chapters.title: Scan a million rows or 4 steps?

scenes.say: Finding one user among a million rows should not mean reading all of them. By the end, you'll make it take four steps, and spot the hidden fifty one queries behind a blog page.

lines.text: Find it in 4 steps, not 1,000,000 reads

scenes.say: Three things today. Make a lookup take four steps, not a million reads. Know when an index backfires. And spot and fix the hidden fifty one queries.
lines: Find a row in 4 steps, not a scan
Spot and fix the N+1 queries

scenes.title: Why is this lookup slow?
scenes.statement: A users table has a million rows. Finding one user by email takes far too long.
scenes.say: Every login looks up a user by email. With a million users, each login crawls. The fix is called an index. We want about four steps, not a million.

scenes.head: Same lookup, a million users
scenes.say: Same lookup, a million users, on one machine. Scanning every row takes seventy two thousand microseconds, about seventy milliseconds. With an index, thirty microseconds. More than two thousand times faster, same answer.

scenes.head: A catalog for your table
scenes.say: Picture a library with a million books and no catalog. To find one title, you walk every shelf. That's a full table scan. Now add a catalog: look up the title, read a shelf number, walk straight there. The catalog is the index.

scenes.head: A B-tree finding user 50
scenes.say: We want user fifty. The catalog is usually a B tree: keys kept sorted. The root page holds thirty and sixty. A page is one block of disk, a few kilobytes. Below it sit three children, one per range. Fifty is between thirty and sixty, so we take the middle one. It holds forty and fifty, plus a pointer to the row. Real pages hold hundreds of keys, so ten million rows need three or four steps.

scenes.head: Why a B-tree, not a hash?
scenes.say: Why a B tree, and not a hash? Equality works in both. Ranges need sorted order, and a hash has none. Order by wants sorted output, and the tree already has it.

scenes.head: No index: scan
scenes.say: I'm using SQLite. Ask it how it will run this lookup. Explain query plan prints the plan. No index exists, so it says scan users. Postgres calls that a Seq Scan.

setup.seed.sql:
CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT, name TEXT, country TEXT, city TEXT);
WITH RECURSIVE c(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i+1 FROM c WHERE i<1000) INSERT INTO users(email,name,country,city) SELECT 'user'||i||'@mail.com','n'||i,CASE i%2 WHEN 0 THEN 'DE' ELSE 'FR' END,'city'||(i%50) FROM c;

scenes.head: Add the index: search
scenes.say: Add one line. Create index builds the sorted tree on email. Same lookup again. Now the plan says search, using the index. Postgres calls that an Index Scan.

scenes.say: Your turn. The index is on email only, sorted by the raw text. One of these filters cannot use it. Which one? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Index on `email`. Which filter can NOT use it?

scenes.head: Three lookups, three plans
scenes.say: The lower one. A function hides the sorted order, so it scans. A pattern starting with a percent sign scans too. A plain range is fine. The fix: an index on lower of email.
That answers our problem. An index turns a scan of a million rows into a few steps.
lines: Index: a few steps, not a scan

scenes.title: When does an index backfire?
scenes.statement: Indexes speed up reads, but every write pays for them. Which indexes earn their cost?

example.output: index the columns you filter, join, sort

scenes.say: So should you index everything? Reads get faster, but every write pays. Take a users table with three indexes and one insert. Which indexes earn their cost?

scenes.head: Every index is extra work
scenes.say: One insert arrives. This team indexes every column, to be safe. The row goes into the table. Then the email index. Then name. Then city. One insert, four writes. Every extra index repeats it, and costs disk too.

scenes.head: Rows fetched: 1 : 20,000 : 500,000
scenes.say: Filter by email: one row comes back. That's selective: few rows match. Filter by city, one of fifty: a million divided by fifty, twenty thousand rows. Filter by country, two values: half a million. An index barely helps.

scenes.head: A phone book is a composite index
scenes.say: A phone book is sorted by last name, then first name. Every Smith sits together, so that lookup is fast. Every John? Scattered across every surname: read it all. A composite index behaves the same: leftmost column first.
Try this one. A composite index on country, then city. You filter only by city. Does the database use it?
scenes.q: Index on `(country, city)`. Query: `WHERE city = 'city7'`. Used?

scenes.head: Skip the leftmost column
scenes.say: No: normally a full scan. The index starts with country, and this filter skips it. Put the column you always filter by first.

setup.seed.sql:
CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT, name TEXT, country TEXT, city TEXT);
WITH RECURSIVE c(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i+1 FROM c WHERE i<1000) INSERT INTO users(email,name,country,city) SELECT 'user'||i||'@mail.com','n'||i,CASE i%2 WHEN 0 THEN 'DE' ELSE 'FR' END,'city'||(i%50) FROM c;

scenes.say: So which indexes earn their cost? Every index costs writes, so index selective columns you filter, join or sort on.
lines: Index selective columns you filter, join, sort

scenes.title: Why does one page run 51 queries?
scenes.statement: A blog page shows 50 posts with author names, and it is slow. Find out why, and fix it.
scenes.say: Users wait a tenth of a second on this blog page, for nothing. Fifty posts, each with its author. Two queries should do it, not fifty one.

scenes.head: A shopping trip
scenes.say: Your blog page shows fifty posts, each with an author name. Picture shopping for fifty items. Fifty trips, one item each? Or one trip with a list? Each trip costs the drive. A database query costs a round trip.

scenes.head: One blog page, many queries
scenes.say: Watch the blog page. First, one query loads fifty posts. That's one. Then, for each post, it asks for the author. Post one, post two, all the way to fifty. That's fifty one queries. At two milliseconds a round trip, that's a hundred and two milliseconds.

scenes.head: The bug, in code
scenes.say: In Python, one query loads the posts. Then a loop asks for each author, one at a time. That loop body runs fifty times. The print shows how many queries ran: fifty one.

panels.code:
posts = query("SELECT * FROM posts LIMIT 50")
for p in posts:
    query("SELECT * FROM authors WHERE id = ?",
          p["author_id"])
print(calls)

setup.app.py:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
db.executescript("CREATE TABLE authors(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE posts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, author_id INT);")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO authors VALUES (?,?)", [(i, "a%d" % i) for i in range(1, 11)])
db.executemany("INSERT INTO posts VALUES (?,?,?)", [(i, "p%d" % i, i % 10 + 1) for i in range(1, 51)])
calls = 0
def query(sql, *args):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return db.execute(sql, args).fetchall()

scenes.say: Predict this before I show you. Those fifty posts have only ten different authors. A batched in query fetches the authors all at once. How many queries now?
scenes.q: 50 posts, 10 distinct authors. Batched `IN` fix: how many queries?

scenes.head: Fix one: batch with IN
scenes.say: Two: the posts, then all ten authors in one go. First, collect the distinct ids. Then one placeholder per id builds the list. A single query fetches every author. The counter prints two.

panels.code:
posts = query("SELECT * FROM posts LIMIT 50")
ids = list({p["author_id"] for p in posts})
slots = ", ".join(["?"] * len(ids))
query(f"SELECT * FROM authors WHERE id IN ({slots})", *ids)
print(calls)

scenes.head: Fix two: let the database join
scenes.say: Or let the database join them. A join glues each post to the author row with the matching id. One query. The counter prints one.

panels.code:
rows = query("""SELECT p.title, a.name
    FROM posts p
    JOIN authors a ON a.id = p.author_id
    LIMIT 50""")
print(calls)

scenes.head: Join or batch?
scenes.say: Most frameworks do both for you. Django's select related is a join: one query, but the author repeats on every post row. Prefetch related is the in query: two queries, each row once. Rails includes picks between the two. Either way, never query inside a loop.
So the fifty one queries were a loop in disguise. Join or batch, and they become one or two.

scenes.title: A page is slow. Where do we start?
scenes.statement: Someone says add an index. How do we find the real cause before changing anything?

example.output: find it, fix one thing, measure

scenes.say: A teammate says the page is slow: add an index. A wrong index slows writes. A slow page, cause unknown. Find it, fix one thing, measure.

scenes.head: Slow page? Follow the order
scenes.say: Here's the order. First, count the queries per request. Fifty identical ones means N plus one. Next, read the plan of the slowest query. Fix one thing. Then measure again.

scenes.head: Read the plan
scenes.say: On Postgres, explain analyze runs the query and prints its plan. A Seq Scan on a big table with a filter is the red flag. An Index Scan means the tree is working. Each step shows estimated rows, a guess from statistics: stored counts of each column's values. Far from actual rows? The stats are stale, so run analyze.
rows: the sorted tree is in use

scenes.say: Quick one. A table has twenty rows, and the plan shows a Seq Scan. Should you add an index? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: 20-row table, plan shows Seq Scan. Add an index?
options: Yes: Seq Scan is a bug

scenes.head: Disk pages read on a 20-row table
scenes.say: No. Twenty rows fit in one disk page, so a scan reads one. An index reads its own page, then the table page: at least two. Tiny tables don't need one. Measure first.
That's where to start. Count the queries, read the plan, fix one thing, measure.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How does an index help? A sorted B tree: about four steps. Why not a hash? A hash only does equality. Ranges need the B tree. When do indexes hurt? Every write updates each index. A composite on country, city? Helps country, not city alone. How do you check? Run explain before and after.
rows: A sorted B-tree: about 4 steps, not a scan
Why a B-tree, not a hash?
Hash: equality only. B-tree: ranges too
Every write updates every index and uses disk

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What's N plus one? One query per row: fifty one queries for fifty posts. How do you spot it? Count the queries per request. The fix? A join, or one batched in query. Is a join always better? No: it repeats the author on every row.
rows: One query per row: 51 queries for 50 posts
A JOIN, or one batched `IN` query
No: it repeats the author on every row

scenes.kicker: How do you read a plan?
scenes.say: How do you read a query plan? Run explain analyze. A Seq Scan on a big table is a red flag. Tiny ones are fine. An Index Scan means the index is doing its job. Estimated rows far from actual? Stale stats, so run analyze.
lines: Seq Scan on a big table: red flag. Tiny: fine.
Index Scan: the index is doing its job.
Estimate far from actual rows: run ANALYZE.

scenes.head: Do this tonight
scenes.say: Try three things. Add an index on email, and compare explain before and after. Then wrap the column in lower, and watch the index stop working. Finally, count the queries on one page of your own app, and fix the loop.
So say this. An index is a sorted tree: a few hops instead of a scan. It costs writes, so index what you filter and sort on. And N plus one is a query in a loop: join, batch, measure.
lines: An index is a sorted tree: few steps, no scan.
It costs writes: index what you filter and sort.
N+1 is a query in a loop: join, batch, measure.
